answer:
The bubble-point pressure is about **96.3 kPa (0.963 bar, 722 mmHg)**.

**Why it isn't Raoult's law:** water and n-hexane are almost completely immiscible as liquids. So a 50/50 mixture is really two liquid phases. Each phase is close to pure, and each exerts its own pure-component vapour pressure no matter what the overall composition is. The bubble point is therefore the sum of the two vapour pressures, P = P_water_sat + P_hexane_sat. The 50/50 split does not enter as long as both liquid phases are present.

| Quantity at 60 °C | Antoine equation | CoolProp (second method) |
|---|---|---|
| P_sat, water | 19.87 kPa | 19.95 kPa |
| P_sat, n-hexane | 76.39 kPa | 76.41 kPa |
| **Bubble-point pressure** | **96.26 kPa** | **96.36 kPa** |

- The first vapour bubble is about 79 mol% hexane and 21 mol% water.
- The total stays below 1 atm (101.3 kPa), so the mixture does not boil at 60 °C at atmospheric pressure. This also fits the known heteroazeotrope boiling point of about 61.6 °C at 1 atm. That figure is from memory; I did not compute it.
- If you wrongly treat the liquid as one ideal solution, Raoult's law gives 0.5·19.9 + 0.5·76.4 ≈ 48 kPa. That is about half the real value and is the common mistake with this question.

The vapour pressures were computed two independent ways, as shown in the table. I neglected the small mutual solubility of water and hexane; it would change the result by well under 1%, but I did not calculate that. No files were created.
